analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 income tax rate cuts permanent instead of letting them expire.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by a single senator with no cosponsors, placed on the Senate calendar, and never brought up for a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2001 tax law (EGTRRA) lowered income tax rates across the board, but by its own terms those rate cuts were set to expire after 2010. This bill would delete that expiration date, making the lower marginal rates permanent. It was introduced by Sen. Lindsey Graham with no cosponsors, placed on the Senate calendar, and never debated or voted on.
analysis.who_benefits: All households with taxable income would keep the lower rates enacted in 2001. The largest dollar gains, however, would go to the highest-income households, who pay taxes at the top marginal rates and would keep those permanently reduced rates rather than seeing them revert in 2011.

how_it_helps.text: Permanently removes the scheduled expiration of the reduced individual income tax rates enacted by the 2001 tax law, so the rates in effect in 2007 would continue instead of reverting after 2010 [S2][S3].
Keeping the lower rates in place means no future tax increase from the scheduled sunset for any household that pays income tax at those rates [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would collect less revenue every year than it would if the rate cuts expired as scheduled. That revenue loss would be made up through larger deficits or through spending cuts or other tax increases later, which fall in practice on future taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: Making the rate cuts permanent locks in lower federal revenue indefinitely, adding to budget deficits rather than allowing the scheduled 2011 reversion to rebuild revenue [S2].

The bill addresses only the rate cuts of the 2001 law and does so without any offset, so the cost lands entirely on the federal budget; the largest dollar benefit flows to the highest earners, who face the top marginal rates [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Ordinary households would keep modestly lower rates, which is a real benefit. But the bill was drafted as a one-line repeal of the 2001 law's sunset, with no offsets, and the biggest dollar gains from permanently preserving the top-rate reductions go to the highest-income taxpayers while the revenue loss adds to deficits. It also does nothing to address the many other provisions of the 2001 law that were still set to expire. A more balanced approach would have weighed the cost of permanence against other uses of that revenue.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and placed on the Senate calendar, but no one ever brought it up for debate or a vote, and the Congress ended without action.

narrative.text: Sen. Lindsey Graham introduced the bill on October 17, 2007, and it was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on October 18 [S1][S5].
No committee was assigned, no cosponsors ever joined, and no further action of any kind was taken before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained much. With no cosponsors and no floor action, the bill was a statement rather than a law; the scheduled 2011 expiration of the rate cuts stood, preserving the federal revenue that permanence would have given up.

for.name: Sen. Lindsey Graham
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2001 tax rate cuts permanent; no other senator joined him.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.role: Senate Majority Leader's office (controlled floor scheduling in the 110th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for debate or a vote after it was placed on the calendar.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsor signed on, so there is no record of partisan support or opposition beyond the lone Republican sponsor.

industries.note: The bill would permanently preserve the reduced top marginal income tax rates, whose largest dollar benefits go to the highest earners. The cost is foregone federal revenue that would otherwise return after the scheduled 2011 expiration, borne through deficits or future taxes.
Every household taxed at the 2001-law rates would keep those lower rates instead of facing the scheduled reversion, though the benefit shrinks as income falls.
